in_window.title: What If You Were Reborn as Your Little Sister’s Baby?
in_window.description:
Tonight you’re fifteen, and you’re yelling at your little sister. She broke your headphones. You call her “Noodle.” She says she wishes you weren’t her brother. Two doors slam 🚪💥

You close your eyes for one second… and open them as a newborn 👶

The woman holding you has your sister’s face. Just eighteen years older. She’s your mom now. And she named you after yourself 😳

Then your best friend walks in. He’s your dad. Your parents walk in. They’re your grandparents. You’re one day old and you already need a nap

She kept your room exactly how you left it, and put your crib inside it. At night she whispers to you about her big brother, and the fight she never got to say sorry for. You cry. She thinks you’re hungry 🍼

So you try everything to tell her. Alphabet blocks that spell NOODLE (Marcus makes noodles). Your old school photo. Mashed peas (it looks like a duck). And the secret handshake nobody else ever knew… 🤜🤛

Your first word is the nickname only you ever called her. A plate hits the floor 🍽️

Years later, you shoot free throws the same weird way. You laugh the same snort. Your grandparents keep staring. And in your old desk drawer, you find a letter she wrote to her brother and never sent ✉️

If you got a second chance with someone you never said sorry to… what would you say first? ❤️

in_window.title: What If You Had 500 Charisma?
in_window.description:
Would you take it? Play this episode's round of the What If Card Game free → https://whatifgame.site/d11

What if you had 500 charisma? You throw a dodgeball straight through the gym window, and Principal Hale, who has never smiled in her life, is already filling out your detention slip. You ask about her fish. Twenty minutes later, the window was nobody's fault, and you walk out with the keys to the vending machine. Most people have about ten charisma. You have five hundred.

At first it's amazing. Mom says yes to a dog after six years of no. The pop quiz turns open-book. The kid who's taken your hat since fourth grade starts carrying your backpack to the bus. The mayor builds a skatepark with your name on it, the governor lets you steer his helicopter, and an envelope comes on White House paper: the President wants to meet you. Then you find out nobody can say no to you. Not even when they want to.

Everyone who has ever met you loves you. You just can't name one person who'd still like you if they had a choice.

Would you take it? Play this episode's round of the What If Card Game free → https://whatifgame.site/d11

What's the first thing you'd ask for? Tell us in the comments.

Is any of this real? The science in this episode:
- People make up their minds about a new face in about a tenth of a second. Judgments of trustworthiness, likeability and competence made after a 100-millisecond look were close to the ones made with no time limit; more time mostly made people more confident. Willis & Todorov (2006), "First impressions: Making up your mind after a 100-ms exposure to a face", Psychological Science 17(7).
- Students guessed they'd have to ask about 11 strangers before 3 agreed to write the word "pickle" in pen in a library book. On average they needed about 5, and 87% of them underestimated how many people would say yes. Bohns, Roghanizad & Xu (2014), "Underestimating our influence over others' unethical behavior and decisions", Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 40(3).
- After talking for the first time, people think the other person liked them less than they really did. Five studies, from strangers in a lab to college dorm mates. Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom & Clark (2018), "The liking gap in conversations: Do people like us more than we think?", Psychological Science 29(11).
- The White House Easter Egg Roll draws tens of thousands of people: more than 30,000 in 2011, and about 40,000 in 2024, according to the White House. AP (2011, 2024).

in_window.title: What If You Got $1 Every Time Someone Lied to You?
in_window.description:
What If You Got $1 Every Time Someone Lied to You?

You ride your bike to Freezy's and ask for a chocolate cone. "Machine's broken," the cashier says. Something crinkles in your hoodie pocket. A dollar bill. It wasn't there a second ago. Behind her, the machine is humming. "It's been broken all day." Another dollar. "It's, like, really broken." Three dollars. A cone costs three dollars.

At first it's amazing. Mom says the cookies are all gone. One dollar, so they're not, and you find them over the fridge in a box that says OATMEAL. The dentist says this won't hurt a bit. Your little sister is worth about three dollars a day. A girl at lunch says her dad invented the chicken nugget, and she's worth eleven dollars a lunch. You pick up a scam call for the first time in your life and keep him talking for twenty minutes. A used-car dealer called Honest Hank runs for mayor, and you sit in the front row of the debate with an empty backpack. By spring there are forty thousand one-dollar bills in your closet, and everybody wants to sit with the kid with the ones. "Love the shoes." One dollar. "We always liked you." One dollar. The richer you get, the more people lie to you.

Then you tell a joke at lunch, and a girl says you're so funny. One dollar. You thought it was a good joke. Your best friend has paid you forty-one times since September. Your mom has paid you three hundred and six. A dollar tells you somebody lied. It never tells you why. And there's one question you've never asked anybody, because you don't want that dollar. On the last day of school, you ask a thousand people at once.

Who in your life would pay you the most, and would you really want to know? Tell us in the comments.

Is any of this real? The science in this episode:
- Mom's line at the store is the most common lie parents tell. Researchers asked 114 parents in the US and 85 in China about lying to their children to get them to behave. 84% in the US and 98% in China said they had, and the most common lie in both countries was threatening to leave a child behind in public. Heyman, Hsu, Fu & Lee (2013), "Instrumental lying by parents in the US and China", International Journal of Psychology 48(6).
- A few people tell most of the lies. In a national survey of 1,000 US adults, 60% said they had told no lies in the past 24 hours, and "almost half of all lies are told by only 5% of subjects." Serota, Levine & Boster (2010), "The prevalence of lying in America: Three studies of self-reported lies", Human Communication Research 36(1).
- Americans reported losing a record $15.9 billion to scams in 2025, up from $12.5 billion the year before. That counts only the losses people reported, across about 3 million fraud reports. Federal Trade Commission, Consumer Sentinel Network data for 2025.
- A dollar bill weighs about one gram, whatever it's worth, so about 454 of them make a pound. (The story's math: the forty thousand ones in the closet come to about 88 pounds.) Bureau of Engraving and Printing, currency FAQ.
- We lie to strangers for ourselves and to friends for them. People kept a diary of every lie they told for a week: 77 students in one study, 70 people from the community in another. They told relatively more self-serving lies to strangers and acquaintances and relatively more kind lies to friends, and they lied less per conversation to the people they were closest to. DePaulo & Kashy (1998), "Everyday lies in close and casual relationships", Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 74(1).

in_window.title: What If It Was -100°C for 10 Years?
in_window.description:
What if it was −100°C (−148°F) for 10 years — and you had to survive it? In this animated survival story, the polar vortex collapses, your city freezes in a single night, and the cold never leaves. How long would you last?

You're the super of an old apartment building. You drain the pipes before they burst, build a stove from a steel drum, and burn the building one apartment at a time. A young mine hoist operator named Iris walks toward your chimney smoke. Then one night, someone knocks on the heating pipe… and you knock back. What follows is ten years of extreme cold survival: a robbery that takes your fire, a nine-mile walk across a frozen city, and a salt mine 650 feet underground where the temperature never drops.

The never-ending winter is our "what if." Everything else is real science of cold survival:
• Why mercury thermometers stop working at −39°C
• Why ordinary steel shatters in arctic cold — and copper doesn't
• Why wet wood plugs a chimney with ice
• Why frozen food never spoils
• Why the frost line goes deeper into the ground every year
• Why a deep salt mine stays around +20°C (68°F) all year round

If you like winter survival stories, arctic survival, "how long would you survive" scenarios and animated what-if videos, this one is for you.

💬 If those five men had never taken your fire — when would you have walked away from it on your own? Tell me in the comments.

in_window.description:
What If Everyone Could Hear Your Thoughts?
Would you take it? Now add the catch: …but it's ten times stronger at family dinners. Yes or hell no?We turned this question into a card game: the What If Card Game. 150 cards, and your friends pick your catch. Play this round free → https://whatifgame.site/p12

What if everyone near you could hear every thought in your head? You're halfway through a quiz when the girl in front of you turns around and asks for a pencil. You hand her one and keep your mouth shut. "She's so pretty." Every head in the room turns to you.

At first it's amazing. Your participation grade goes from a C to an A, and you never raise your hand. You win an argument with your little sister without saying a word. One bite of a taco and everybody in line orders three. Companies fly you in to test their toys, and the biggest pop star on the planet wants you on stage in front of twenty thousand people, because you're the one person who can't fake liking her song. Then your best friend hears what you really think.

You don't get to pick what you think. Nobody does. Everybody else just gets to keep it to themselves.

Would you take it? Now add the catch: …but it's ten times stronger at family dinners. Yes or hell no?
We turned this question into a card game: the What If Card Game. 150 cards, and your friends pick your catch.

Play this round free → https://whatifgame.site/p12

Who's the one person you'd never want hearing your thoughts? Tell us in the comments.

Is any of this real? The science in this episode:
- In 2025, Stanford scientists decoded sentences that four people with paralysis only imagined saying, using implants in the motor cortex. When participants silently counted shapes, the decoder picked up the numbers without being asked, so the team added an imagined password that keeps it off until it's thought. Kunz, Meschede-Krasa et al. (2025), Cell.
- People who wrote down every lie they told for a week told one or two a day on average, and about one in four was told only for the other person's sake. DePaulo, Kirkendol, Kashy, Wyer & Epstein (1996), "Lying in everyday life", Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 70(5).
- People who said their thoughts out loud for five minutes while trying not to think of a white bear still thought of it more than once a minute. Wegner, Schneider, Carter & White (1987), "Paradoxical effects of thought suppression", Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 53(1).
- Across 10 studies and more than 13,000 secrets, people's minds wandered to their secrets far more often than they ever had to hide them. Slepian, Chun & Mason (2017), "The experience of secrecy", Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 113(1).
- The capital of Australia is Canberra, not Sydney. Australian Government, "Our country" (australia.gov.au).

Would you teach the future everything you know?

in_window.title: Boiling Point: 5 Days Survival
in_window.description:
What if the temperature hit 173°F tomorrow? Plastic goes soft. Birds fall out of the sky. Dry grass catches fire from a single spark. And the only cold place left is under the ground.

This is a stickman survival short movie: five days in your grandfather's old storm cellar, on a farm at the edge of a pine forest, while a superflare bakes the Earth. Two and a half gallons of water, a father who says heat has never scared him, and the rules that keep you alive when the air outside could cook you.

PART 2 already on channel - https://youtu.be/_rdjVftWRZk?is=m4xavJjP3MIhD_IQ

This is a fictional story. The science in it is real:
• 173°F (78°C) is hotter than any air temperature ever measured on Earth.
• An air conditioner doesn't make cold. It pushes heat outside, and when the outside air is hot enough, there's nowhere left to push it.
• Ten feet down, the ground stays at about the same temperature all year round.
• In extreme heat you can sweat away about half a gallon an hour. When the water in your body runs out, the sweat stops, and heat stroke follows.
• To cool someone with heat stroke, put wet cloths on the neck, under the arms and in the groin, where big blood vessels run close to the skin.

in_window.title: You Spent 10 Years in a Bunker. You Only Needed 5.
in_window.description:
What would it actually take to survive 10 years in a bunker after a nuclear war?

October 14. Omaha disappears in a flash 60 miles away, and you have about an hour before the fallout reaches your farm. Your only chance is the shelter your grandfather built under the barn in 1962 — a concrete room 12 feet underground, with an old logbook, a hand pump and a wall of wheat buckets.

You go down. Then you stay down. For 3,650 days.

In this animated survival story you'll see, step by step, how a real fallout shelter keeps you alive: how radiation fades with time, how you filter air, store water, make power and ration food — and what happens when the supplies, the batteries and the filters start running out.

But the hardest part isn't the bunker. It's the voices. A stranger begging at the air pipe. A man named Dutch who wants what you have. A fire on top of your hatch. And every Sunday, the same knock on the steel: shave and a haircut… two bits.

Would you have answered the knock? Tell me in the comments.

Things become even more complicated when you discover mysterious writing left behind by a previous survivor, a secret emergency beacon, and a rescue ship approaching the island. What happened to the last man who washed ashore? Why does the village leader refuse to trust outsiders? And what happens when you’re forced to choose between returning home and protecting the people who saved you?

This 30-day survival adventure explores friendship, trust, mysterious island traditions, unexpected discoveries, and the difficult choices that come with being the only outsider in a hidden community. Could you earn all 100 spears before time runs out?

Then his phone buzzed: two stats quizzes below passing, and his financial aid under review. That afternoon, Spencer Kingsley—top of every class, every professor's favorite—waved an A+ in Ezra's face while the whole room laughed. Over Spencer's head, in red: 91.

Ezra had the horsepower. He'd just never done the work. So his mom dropped his phone in the cookie jar, and his best friend Rudy drilled him on fractions until one in the morning. Then Professor Lin announced the State Scholars Cup: 240 students, 31 colleges, one full scholarship worth about $78,000. Ezra raised his hand. Spencer laughed and named himself the benchmark. And in the front row of the final sat a man in a charcoal suit, checking his watch.

in_window.description:
▶ NEW VIDEO: What If You Were the Only Man on an Island of 100 Amazons? https://youtu.be/UtXsABU4Cek

What if you were frozen for 1,000 years? This what if animation wakes you up in 3026 with a hundred dollars in the bank, a robot that is more scared than you, and a mystery: somebody kept your pod cold on purpose.

It was supposed to be one night. A lab paid you a hundred bucks. A thousand years of compound interest later, you're the richest person in history. Too bad pizza costs fourteen million a slice, nobody understands your English, and the bank would very much like you to be dead. Then you find a note signed J.

So... who would keep your pod cold for a thousand years? Tell us in the comments.

Real facts in this video
• Moss frozen in Antarctic permafrost for over 1,500 years grew again in the lab: Roads, Longton & Convey, Current Biology 24(6), 2014. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2014.01.053
• English from the year 1026 is unreadable today: the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle entry for that year reads "Her for Ælfric biscop to Rome" ("In this year bishop Ælfric went to Rome"), manuscript D.
• In 1790 Benjamin Franklin left 1,000 pounds to Boston and told the city to wait 200 years; by 1990 the fund was worth about $4.5 million: Education Week, April 1990. https://www.edweek.org/education/benjamin-franklins-penny-saved-means-training-dollars-for-2-cities/1990/04
• US consumer prices rose more than 30 times since 1913 (CPI-U 9.9 in 1913, 313.7 in 2024): U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. https://www.bls.gov/cpi/
• The Moon drifts away from Earth by about 3.8 cm a year, measured by bouncing lasers off the Apollo reflectors: NASA. https://eclipse.gsfc.nasa.gov/help/ApolloLaser.html
• Vint Cerf, one of the fathers of the internet, warned in 2015 of a "digital Dark Age": files nobody keeps copying become unreadable: BBC, February 2015. https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-31450389

Everyone in this video is fictional.

in_window.title: What If You Turned Into A Girl?
in_window.description:
What if you woke up one morning and suddenly turned into a girl? 🎀 You look in the mirror and barely recognize yourself. Your hair is longer, your voice sounds completely different, and even your clothes have changed. But the strangest part? Everyone remembers you as a girl, and you're the only one who knows you used to be a guy!

In this animated what-if scenario, we imagine life after an impossible overnight transformation: learning to navigate a completely different appearance, dealing with unexpected attention, joining girls' group chats, and discovering how differently your friends might treat you. From awkward school encounters to shopping adventures and unexpected crushes, everyday life could become surprisingly complicated.

Would you enjoy your new life or immediately search for a way to turn back? Imagine discovering that your old best friend barely talks to you anymore, while people you've never been close to suddenly consider you their best friend. And what happens when a boy asks you on a date, or you realize your entire past has somehow been rewritten?

This strange transformation adventure explores identity, friendship, relationships, social expectations, and what it means to see the world from someone else's perspective. With a new appearance but all your old memories, would you still feel like the same person?

And if you finally discovered a way to become a guy again, would you take it—or would you choose to stay a girl?

If you enjoyed this adventure, watch our other videos:

Every time the last swimmer touches the wall, the race starts over, and everyone forgets except you. Tiredness, injuries and hunger are wiped every time, you never get older, and your body keeps every bit of muscle it builds. The only way out is to touch the wall before him.

▶ NEW VIDEO: What If You Were the Only Man on an Island of 100 Amazons? https://youtu.be/UtXsABU4Cek

What if you could see who loves you? This what if animation gives you three days of hearts above everyone's head: who hates you, who doesn't care, and who loves you 100%.

Imagine you wake up tomorrow, and there's a heart above everyone's head. Black means they don't like you. Gray means you don't matter to them. Red means they like you. And 100% means they're in love with you.

But there's a catch: day one, you only see black hearts. Day two, gray. Day three, red. Then they vanish for a whole year. Your best friend turns out to be at −100%. And the person who loves you 100% is the last person you'd ever guess.

Along the way, the real science of how to tell if someone likes you: a real smile versus a polite one, pupils that widen, and why believing someone likes you can make it come true.

So... whose heart would you check first? Tell us in the comments.

Real facts in this video
• A real smile usually also tightens the muscles around the eyes (the "Duchenne smile"), a polite one often only moves the mouth: Ekman, Davidson & Friesen, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 58(2), 1990. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.58.2.342
• Social circles come in layers of about 5, about 15 and about 150 people: Zhou, Sornette, Hill & Dunbar, Proceedings of the Royal Society B 272(1561), 2005. https://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2004.2970
• People who were led to believe a partner liked them behaved more warmly, and the partner came to like them more: Curtis & Miller, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 51(2), 1986. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.51.2.284
• Mutual gaze between dogs and their owners raised oxytocin in both: Nagasawa et al., Science 348(6232), 2015. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1261022
• About two thirds of cats tested (64% of kittens) were securely attached to their owners, close to the share seen in human infants: Vitale, Behnke & Udell, Current Biology 29(18), 2019. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2019.08.036
• Pupils tend to widen when we look at something or someone we find interesting or pleasant: Hess, Scientific American 212(4), 1965. https://doi.org/10.1038/scientificamerican0465-46

Everyone in this video is fictional.

in_window.description:
What If You Could See Who Is Secretly Attracted to You?

You get on the bus, and the only empty seat is next to Sloane Avery. "Um. No. Find another seat." She's glowing. Bright pink, head to toe, like a neon sign, and nobody else on the bus even looks. "There aren't any." "Then stand." She gets brighter. By the time you sit down, she's so bright the window is pink. She has no idea you can see it.

At first it's amazing. In science you pick your partner by looking for pink. There's a note in your locker that says "I think you're cute," and down the hall one girl is as pink as a flamingo. Your little sister's best friend glows like a night-light and gives you all her fruit snacks. You've never asked a girl anything in your life, and now you just ask, because if she's glowing it isn't really asking. Forty lights at the county fair. A seat at the eighth-grade table. A ride on the fire truck in the Christmas parade. Sixty-three carnations on Valentine's Day, and not one of them signed. You know exactly who sent every single one.

Then one morning a light you were counting on just isn't there anymore, and you have no idea when it stopped. The glow shows you who likes you. It shows you everything else, too. Your best friend has loved the same girl since fourth grade, and she glows for you. And at the spring dance, with four hundred kids watching, you walk away from seventy-one lights toward the one that's off.

Would you want to see who's secretly attracted to you, or would you rather not know? Tell us in the comments.

Is any of this real? The science in this episode:
- The people who are liked, and don't like back, tell the unhappier stories. College students wrote accounts of one-sided love from both sides. The would-be lovers looked back with both good and painful feelings; the accounts of the people who'd been liked were "more uniformly negative." They saw themselves as innocent but still felt guilty, and didn't know how they were supposed to act. Baumeister, Wotman & Stillwell (1993), "Unrequited love: On heartbreak, anger, guilt, scriptlessness, and humiliation", Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 64(3).
- About two out of three couples were friends first. Across seven samples of nearly 1,900 university students and adults, 68% said their current or most recent romantic relationship began as a friendship. Stinson, Cameron & Hoplock (2021), "The Friends-to-Lovers Pathway to Romance", Social Psychological and Personality Science.

in_window.description:
What If You Could Hear What Everyone Says Behind Your Back?
Would you take it? Play this episode's round of the What If Card Game free →  https://whatifgame.site/d8

What if you could hear every word anyone says about you when you're not there? You get up from the lunch table, and three tables away a voice lands right behind your ear. It's your best friend. "Honestly? I can't stand him." When you get back to the table, he's saving you his pudding.

At first it's amazing. You find out your little sister thinks you're the best, though she'd never tell you. The girl behind you in science would say yes if you asked her to the dance, so you ask. You win class president by two hundred votes. You pull an old man's dog out of a pond, and that night two million strangers are talking about you at once. Then you hear the group chat.

Everybody talks about somebody who isn't there. One day, the voice you hear is your own.

Whose voice would you listen for first? Tell us in the comments.

Is any of this real? The science in this episode:
- The average person spends about 52 minutes a day talking about someone who isn't there, and almost three-quarters of it is neutral, not mean. 467 people wore recorders that sampled their everyday conversations. Robbins & Karan (2019), "Who Gossips and How in Everyday Life?", Social Psychological and Personality Science.
- When teens aged 13 to 18 saw photos with lots of likes, including their own photos, the brain's reward circuitry (the nucleus accumbens) was more active. Sherman, Payton, Hernandez, Greenfield & Dapretto (2016), "The Power of the Like in Adolescence", Psychological Science 27(7).
- When a story is passed from person to person, each retelling gets shorter and simpler, and a few details get sharper. Psychologists call it leveling and sharpening. Allport & Postman (1947), The Psychology of Rumor.
- When you say something bad about someone, the people listening start to connect that trait with you. Skowronski, Carlston, Mae & Crawford (1998), "Spontaneous Trait Transference: Communicators Take On the Qualities They Describe in Others", Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 74(4).

How long until you reach the end of everything? About 104 nights. 🌙

Would you wait that long for a friend? Tell me in the comments.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🔬 REAL-LIFE CHECK
The story is fiction. The science is real:

• Most people can only survive about 3 days without water.
  Source: Healthline — https://www.healthline.com/health/food-nutrition/how-long-can-you-live-without-water

• English from about a thousand years ago (Old English) is largely incomprehensible to modern speakers without study.
  Source: Wikipedia — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_English

• In about 50,000 years, Niagara Falls will have eroded the remaining 32 km to Lake Erie and ceased to exist. In about 100,000 years, the stars' motion makes many constellations unrecognizable.
• Within about a million years, Earth will likely have had a huge supervolcanic eruption and been hit by a ~1 km asteroid, and the red supergiant Betelgeuse will likely have exploded as a supernova.
• In about 10 million years, the Red Sea may flood Africa's widening East African Rift, opening a new ocean. In about 50 million years, Africa's collision with Eurasia closes the Mediterranean and raises mountains like the Himalayas.
• In about 600 million years, the Moon will be too far away for total solar eclipses. In about 5.4 billion years, the Sun starts becoming a red giant that destroys Mercury, Venus and possibly Earth, before ending as a white dwarf.
• There's a 50% chance the Andromeda galaxy will have collided with the Milky Way within about 10 billion years.
• In 100–150 billion years, every galaxy beyond our own group disappears from view. By about 120 trillion years, every star has run out of fuel. A black hole with the Sun's mass takes about 1.16 × 10^67 years to evaporate.
  Source for these: Wikipedia, Timeline of the far future — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_far_future

• The math: night n lasts 8 × 10^(n−1) hours, and each new night is about 9 times longer than all the nights before it combined. After night 104, about a googol (10^100) years have passed.

in_window.description:
You walk into the kitchen on Saturday morning, and there's a name floating above your mom's head. Glowing gold letters: "Daniel." Your dad's name. Cute. Then your dad lowers his newspaper, and above his head there's a different name. "Claire." Everyone has one: the first name of the person they'd be happiest with for the rest of their life. You can see them all. Everyone's soulmate. Except your own.

In this story, you'll find out where the idea of an "other half" comes from, why the odds of finding one random soulmate would be about one in ten thousand, why most people marry someone who lived just a few blocks away, what love actually does to your brain, why couples' hearts can beat in sync, how 36 questions can make two strangers feel close, and how good we really are at spotting a lie.

Would YOU want to see the name above your own head? 👇

Every power has a price.

0:00 The Names
0:48 The Rules
1:40 The Love Doctor
2:43 The Wrong Names
3:26 Monday Morning
4:14 Claire
5:32 The Dance
6:47 A Red Thread
7:57 One Whisper
9:34 Ten Years
10:38 The Bench
12:20 New Rules

Science in this video:
- Plato's Symposium (about 2,400 years ago): Aristophanes' myth of humans split in half, the origin of the "other half"
- The red thread of fate: an East Asian legend of two people destined to meet
- With one random soulmate each, only about 1 in 10,000 people would ever find theirs (Randall Munroe, What If?, 2012)
- Bossard (1932): in 5,000 Philadelphia marriage licenses, a third of couples lived within five blocks of each other
- The spotlight effect: people think twice as many others notice them as actually do (Gilovich, Medvec & Savitsky, 2000)
- Intense romantic love activates the brain's reward system (Fisher, Aron & Brown, 2005)
- Couples sitting together tend to synchronize their heart rates and breathing (Ferrer & Helm, UC Davis, 2013)
- The mere-exposure effect: we tend to like what we see more often (Zajonc, 1968)
- The 36 questions that can create closeness between strangers (Aron et al., 1997)
- Couples who stayed together answered each other's "bids" for attention far more often (Gottman)
- The prefrontal cortex keeps maturing until about the mid-twenties
- People tell about 1–2 lies a day, and we spot lies only about 54% of the time (DePaulo et al., 1996; Bond & DePaulo, 2006)
- "Butterflies": adrenaline diverts blood away from the stomach
- Social rejection activates some of the same brain regions as physical pain (Eisenberger et al., 2003)
- Asking more follow-up questions makes people like you more (Huang et al., Harvard, 2017)
- Stable couples have about 5 positive interactions for every negative one during conflict (Gottman)

THE REAL NUMBERS
• On June 27, 1988, in Atlantic City, the real Mike Tyson knocked out Michael Spinks in 91 seconds, in front of a crowd of about 21,785.
• Tyson won his first 19 pro fights by knockout.
• In 1986, at 20, he became the youngest heavyweight champion in history. The Spinks win made him 35-0.

• In 1987, before the line got shortened to "punched in the mouth", Tyson said: "Everybody has plans until they get hit for the first time."

At 4:12 PM the wave comes over the pool deck. Theo, the lifeguard, pulls you into the hotel elevator with a little girl named Ava, and then the sea comes in after you.

0:00 The Wave (4:12 PM)
0:35 Rule 1: Never Take the Elevator
1:26 Rule 2: Never Jump In After Someone
2:21 Rule 3: The Higher, the Better
2:49 Rule 4: When the Sea Pulls Back, Run
4:21 Rule 5: The First Wave Isn't the Biggest
6:09 Rule 6: Never Push a Door That Opens In
7:34 Rule 7: Pick a Meeting Place

Subscribe for the next story.

The story is made up. The safety facts in it are real:
• Never use an elevator in an emergency; when the power goes, it stops where it is (NFPA, Ready.gov)
• Most elevator roof hatches lock from the outside, so passengers can't climb into the shaft (ASME A17.1 elevator safety code)
• Elevators aren't watertight; floodwater gets in at the doors (elevator industry flood guidance)
• Every elevator must have an emergency phone (ASME A17.1)
• Elevators don't free-fall: a safety brake grips the rails if a car drops (ASME A17.1 car safeties)
• Elevator glass is laminated, so it cracks but holds together (ASME A17.1)
• Water pushes on glass harder the deeper it is (hydrostatic pressure)
• Never jump in after someone in moving water: reach, throw, row, go (American Red Cross)
• Holding something that floats keeps you alive in moving water (NOAA, National Weather Service)
• When you can't get out, go up: the third floor or higher of a reinforced concrete building, the higher the better (FEMA P-646, vertical evacuation)
• When the sea suddenly pulls back from a beach, a tsunami is minutes away (NOAA, International Tsunami Information Center)
• The water running back out is as dangerous as the wave coming in, and much of the harm is the debris it carries (NOAA, National Weather Service)
• Near the shore a tsunami still moves at about 20 to 30 mph, faster than anyone can run (NOAA)
• A tsunami comes in like a tide that won't stop rising, not like a breaking surf wave (NOAA, National Weather Service)
• The first wave of a tsunami is often not the biggest, and waves keep coming for hours (NOAA, National Weather Service)
• Six inches of moving water can knock an adult down (National Weather Service, Turn Around Don't Drown)
• In many tall buildings, stair doors lock from the stairwell side, with re-entry only on some floors (NFPA 101, International Building Code)
• Big exit doors must swing outward, because a crowd pushing on a door that opens toward it holds it shut (NFPA 101 Life Safety Code)
• In a crowd crush, the people at the front can't step back; the push comes from behind (crowd safety research, G. Keith Still)
• Families who pick a meeting place before a disaster find each other faster (FEMA, Ready.gov "Make a Plan")

The science bit is real: it's called the spotlight effect. In a famous study, college students wore an embarrassing T-shirt into a room full of people. They guessed about half the room noticed. Really, it was less than one in four.
Source: Gilovich, Medvec & Savitsky (2000), "The spotlight effect in social judgment: An egocentric bias in estimates of the salience of one's own actions and appearance," Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 78(2), 211-222.

in_window.title: What If You Could Read Everyone's LAST Text Message?
in_window.description:
The lunch lady is one nugget request away from moving to Canada. Your best friend is begging strangers for the bio answers. The most popular senior in school is filming a video about living without his phone while it sits at two percent. You know all of this because everyone's last text floats over their head in a little grey bubble, with a tiny timestamp underneath, and nobody else can see a single one. Yours never shows up. Not even in a mirror.

By Tuesday your friend Mateo has turned it into a five-dollar business. By Wednesday the whole school is sure you hack phones, the vice principal has yours sealed in a ziploc bag, and the only person not sliding her desk away is Sloane, the girl across the aisle in English, who works you out with three test texts. Then she takes you to her nana's house. Over the old woman's head sits one bubble that hasn't moved in twenty-six days. On Saturday it finally changes, and it's the last thing you wanted to read.

If you could read just one person's bubble for the rest of your life — your crush, your teacher, or your grandparents — whose would you pick?

0:00 Nuggets and Canada
0:34 Two percent battery
2:12 Ask the Hoodie, five bucks a question
3:20 A rumor with timestamps
4:42 Bait in English class
5:54 A bubble that never moves
7:35 Nine thousand for a new roof
9:43 Eight minutes to noon
12:06 The driveway
13:19 One text of your own

Real things hiding in this story
• The first text message ever was "Merry Christmas," typed on a computer by engineer Neil Papworth on 3 December 1992 and received on an Orbitel 901 phone. That phone could not send anything back (History.com, NPR).
• MIT researchers followed about 126,000 stories on Twitter. False ones reached people roughly six times faster than true ones (Vosoughi, Roy & Aral, Science, 2018).
• In McAfee's 2023 voice-cloning tests, a clip of about three seconds was enough to produce an 85% voice match.
• The "grandparent scam" is a real FBI term: a fake grandchild in trouble, a fake lawyer, a courier at the door for cash. In the FBI's 2024 report, people over 60 reported close to $4.9 billion in losses to fraud (IC3 2024).
• In December 2024 the FBI advised families to agree on a secret word or phrase to check that a voice on the phone is really theirs (IC3 PSA I-120324).

Mateo, Wade, Sloane and Nana Lois are made up, and nobody is reading the bubble over your head. But if your grandparents have never heard of a family code word, tonight is a good night to pick one.

What if you could see everyone's luck? You wake up one morning and there's a number floating over your head: three percent. Your little sister, who has never lost a game of Uno in her life, is at ninety-two. Your mum, five months out of work, is at two. And the old man at the bus stop, who in the last ten seconds has been hit by a pigeon, dropped his phone in a puddle and watched his bus drive away without him, is at ninety-nine.

At first it's amazing. Your luck is three percent, but nobody said your luck had to be the luck that counts. So for one week, your sister makes every choice you have. She picks the canteen queue, the last slice of pizza, the only bus that isn't cancelled, and the answers to a quiz you didn't study for. Then she reaches into the school raffle jar and pulls out your ticket. First prize: a games console. Then she loses a game of Uno, and her number starts to drop.

Every win you had that week was paid for by somebody. And a box at the top of your mum's wardrobe is about to tell you why your own number has been stuck at three for eleven years.

• Ancient Greek athletes sometimes competed without clothing, and the word "gymnasium" comes from the Greek "gymnos", meaning naked. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gymnasium_(ancient_Greece)
• Body lice live mainly in clothing and can spread epidemic typhus.
• Red ochre is a natural earth pigment that people have used for thousands of years.

in_window.description:
¿Y si la ropa nunca se hubiera inventado? Sin abrigo, nadie habría cruzado el frío, y América se habría quedado vacía. Ni tú, ni tu ciudad, ni este idioma existirían. Subimos piso por piso para ver cómo sería ese mundo: el frío, el sol, los pies descalzos, los mosquitos… y quién inventaría la primera prenda.

- Origen de la ropa (genética de los piojos de la ropa, hace 83.000-170.000 años): Toups et al., 2011, Molecular Biology and Evolution.
- Zona termoneutral del cuerpo desnudo (~27 °C) y temblor (hasta ~5 veces el gasto en reposo): Haman, 2006.
- Temperatura media de la Tierra: ~15 °C (NASA / NOAA).
- Poblamiento de América por Beringia (hace ~15.000-20.000 años).
- Piel oscura y melanina como protección solar: Jablonski y Chaplin, 2000; Rogers et al., 2004.
- Quemadura solar en menos de 15 minutos con índice UV alto: OMS / EPA.
- Temperatura del asfalto bajo el sol (más de 60 °C): Vanos et al., 2016.
- Callos que protegen sin quitar sensibilidad: Holowka et al., 2019, Nature.
- Malaria (~600.000 muertes al año): OMS, World Malaria Report.
- ~40 % de la población mundial vive en los trópicos: State of the Tropics Report, 2014. La cifra de 3 mil millones es una estimación para esta historia alternativa.
- Domesticación del algodón (hace ~7.000 años).

in_window.title: What If You Could See How Scared Everyone Is of You?
tags: what if you could see how scared everyone is of you
what if you could see who's scared of you
what if you could see who is scared of you
what if you could see everyone's fear
in_window.description:
What if you could see how scared everyone is of you? A number floats above every head: how scared that person is. Of you.
The guy who locked you in a locker in sixth grade is at 92%. Your best friend is at 4. Your mom jumps to 41 every time you open the fridge.

So you do the logical thing: you play hot and cold. With people. The number climbs when you get close to whatever they're hiding from you, so you follow it. A teacher's desk drawer. A missing pudding. A phone screen. You start a notebook called THE LIST. By Friday every table in the cafeteria is scared of you, and your best friend isn't scared of you at all. That's the worse one.

HOW THE NUMBER WORKS
- Only you can see it. The tag says SCARED OF YOU, and the counter stops at 99.
- It climbs as you get closer to whatever a person is hiding from you: a place, a thing, a word.
- Step back, and it drops again. Hot and cold.
- Say the right word out loud, and somebody's number goes through the roof. Try "pudding."
- If they tell you themselves, it falls back to calm at once. There's nothing left to hide.

WHO'S IN THIS STORY
- You are Milo, a guy who says sorry to doors. Your own number starts at zero.
- Brick, who once locked you in a locker for forty minutes: 92%.
- Theo, your best friend: 4%. Rude, honestly.
- Mom: 3%, until you open the fridge.
- Mr. Hale and his desk drawer: 12, then 30, then 70.
- Tyler and a missing pudding. Harper and her phone. Jayden and a pair of headphones.
- Rosa, the lunch lady: zero, all week.

ALSO IN THIS VIDEO
- Your scariest face, tested in the school bathroom mirror.
- A fire extinguisher you check behind you, just in case.
- A pizza box that was never supposed to be found.
- A sketchbook from sixth grade.

WHAT THE STORY IS REALLY ABOUT
Under the jokes, this is a story about secrets, power and trust: what it does to you to know what everyone is hiding, and what it does to them. Why would a bully be scared of the person he bullied? Is it good news when your best friend isn't scared of you at all? And once everybody's secrets are in your notebook, what are you supposed to do with them?

The number isn't about how scary you are. It's about what they could lose because of you.

Who do you think would have the highest number above their head for you? Tell us in the comments.

GOOD TO KNOW
This is a fictional animated story for teens and up. It isn't a guide to reading people or to getting back at a bully. The scared-of-you percentage is a story device for talking about secrets and forgiveness.

ABOUT STUCKMILO
StuckMilo makes animated what-if stories about school, friends and family, told to you, as if the power were yours. In every story Milo gets stuck with one strange power: something floating above every head that only he can see. A number. A tag. An hourglass. Funny first, honest by the end. Superpowers not included. Consequences are.

You're stuck in a time loop. Same day, forever. The only way out? Land one clean hit on Bruce Lee. In his prime.

Hong Kong, 1972. You're eighteen, a film extra whose whole job is to get hit by Bruce Lee and fall down nicely. Then the day starts again. Rain on a tin roof. A knock on the door. "Eat. Big day." A block doesn't count. A graze doesn't count. You keep every memory, and nobody else keeps any.

How many loops would it take you to land one punch? 👇

2:37 Plan B: learn every move

6:16 The way of the intercepting fist
7:08 Loop 61,214
8:43 The morning after

THE REAL STUFF
• Bruce Lee showed his famous one-inch punch at the 1964 Long Beach International Karate Championships, knocking a volunteer backwards from about an inch away.
• His fighting philosophy is called Jeet Kune Do, "the way of the intercepting fist": hit the attack while it is still starting.
• As a teenager in Hong Kong he trained in Wing Chun.
• He criticised rigid set patterns, calling them "the classical mess".
• It takes a person roughly a fifth to a quarter of a second to react to something they see.
• Studies of expert tennis players show they read where a serve is going from the server's body before the ball is hit.
• The "10,000 kicks" quote is widely attributed to Bruce Lee.

This is a fictional animated story made for entertainment. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or connected to Bruce Lee, his family or his estate.

You step outside in your favorite hoodie, and the whole street stops and stares. In this world, humans never invented clothes, so for once, you are the weird one. Where would you keep your keys? How would anyone survive winter? And how do scientists know when clothes were really invented? The answer involves lice.

0:55 1.2 million years ago: losing our fur
2:01 How lice dated the first clothes
2:30 The bus, towels and bags

Our numbers and sources:
- Losing body hair and darker skin: around 1.2 million years ago, based on the MC1R skin-color gene (Rogers, Iltis and Wooding, Current Anthropology, 2004).
- Humans have about as many hair follicles per square centimeter as chimpanzees; most of our hairs are just very fine.
- Oldest directly dated shoes: Fort Rock sandals, Oregon, about 9,200 to 10,500 years old (University of Oregon).
- Toe bones: human toes became weaker around 40,000 years ago, a sign of regular shoe use (Trinkaus, Journal of Archaeological Science, 2005).
- Lice: body lice split from head lice at least 83,000 and possibly 170,000 years ago (Toups et al., Molecular Biology and Evolution, 2011).
- Thermoneutral zone: a resting unclothed person stays comfortable around 28 degrees Celsius (range often given as 27 to 32).
- Oymyakon, Siberia: one of the coldest permanently inhabited places; winter temperatures regularly fall below minus 50 degrees Celsius.
- Red ochre pigment used by humans more than 100,000 years ago (for example Blombos Cave, South Africa).
- Ötzi the Iceman: died in the Alps about 5,300 years ago; 61 tattoos; clothing from at least five animal species (O'Sullivan et al., Scientific Reports, 2016).
- Gymnasium comes from the Greek gymnos, naked; athletes at the ancient Olympic Games competed nude.
- Global apparel market: about 1.7 to 1.8 trillion dollars in 2024 (market estimates vary). Roughly 100 billion garments are made each year (estimates range from 80 to 150 billion).
- FKK (Freikörperkultur, free body culture) in Germany dates back more than 100 years.
- Dyed flax fibers about 30,000 years old from Dzudzuana Cave, Georgia (Kvavadze et al., Science, 2009).

in_window.description:
This is Earth at night, and half of it is dark. No London, no Moscow, no Chicago, no Tokyo. In this world, humans never invented clothes, and that one missing invention redraws the whole map. Hazel keeps a ledger of everything the world loses and everything it gets to keep.
 
⏱️ CHAPTERS
0:00 Earth at night, minus half
0:46 The naked years
1:10 The louse clue
1:32 The Morocco cave
1:58 Too cold to leave
2:31 Following the reindeer
3:12 The Arctic and the Americas
3:41 Australia still happens
4:10 Beads instead of outfits
4:57 Life in the sun
5:22 No seams, no lice
5:45 Napoleon and the lice
6:14 Paper made of clothes
7:02 The loom that led to computers
8:02 Rickets
8:30 Hazel's final ledger
9:00 The hoodie
9:50 Earth at night, the real one
10:08 Your turn
 
💬 If you could un-invent one thing, what would it be, and what breaks first? Tell me in the comments.
 
🔬 THE SCIENCE
- Our ancestors lost most of their body hair about 1.2 million years ago.
- Body lice (which live in clothes) split from head lice at least 83,000 and possibly 170,000 years ago (Toups et al., 2010, Molecular Biology and Evolution).
- Bone tools for working hides, 90,000 to 120,000 years old, were found in Contrebandiers Cave, Morocco, next to bones of animals skinned for fur.
- An unclothed, resting person is comfortable at only about 28 to 32 °C. Hard shivering can raise energy use four- to fivefold.
- People lived north of the Arctic Circle at the Yana site in Siberia about 32,000 years ago; sewing needles were found there.
- People reached northern Australia by about 65,000 years ago (Madjedbebe).
- 33 shell beads from Bizmoune Cave, Morocco, are 142,000 to 150,000 years old.
- About 500,000 soldiers entered Russia with Napoleon in 1812. In a Vilnius mass grave, 29% of the soldiers tested showed typhus or trench fever.
- European paper was made from cloth rags for centuries, Gutenberg's Bible mostly on rag-linen paper. In the 1600s England required burials in wool to save linen for paper; wood-pulp paper took over in the 1800s.
- Jacquard's punched-card loom inspired Babbage's Analytical Engine and Ada Lovelace's "weaves algebraical patterns." Punched cards counted the 1890 US census, the start of what became IBM.
- Rickets was common for centuries in the Netherlands; researchers name heavy clothing as one factor.
The reindeer trip's day-by-day details are illustrative. Everything else is real.
 
🦉 Hoo Knew? is an animated "what if" channel. Hazel the owl keeps score, Chris tells the story, and every answer is backed by real science. Subscribe for a new what-if every week.

in_window.description:
What if humans had never invented clothes? At forty below zero, every animal in the Ice Age is wearing its survival — the reindeer, the mammoth, even the wolf. Only one creature is standing there naked: you.
Humans are tropical animals in a frozen world, so how did a hairless ape survive winters that killed animals built for the cold?
The answer is an invention we put on every morning without thinking — and the witness that dates it isn't a fossil, it's an insect. Body lice live only inside clothing, and their DNA says we started wearing it about 170,000 years ago.
From scraped and smoked hides that failed in the wind, to a tiny bone needle in Siberia 40,000 years ago that let us sew a second skin — this is the real story of how clothes turned trapped air into survival, why wet cold kills faster than deep cold, and how a man named Ötzi crossed the Alps 5,300 years ago wearing half the animals of his world.
By 31,000 years ago, that sewn suit carried humans above the Arctic Circle. Every animal on Earth is born wearing its survival. Humans are the only animal that has to build theirs.

in_window.description:
What If Humans Never Invented Clothes?

When did humans start wearing clothes, and why? A parasite's DNA, a Moroccan cave full of bone tools and a sewing needle point to an answer that isn't just "we were freezing." We also ask what our species would look like if we had never dressed.
All research and sources are linked below.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Your Outfit Is a Portable Tropical Climate
1:13 Why "We Were Freezing" Doesn't Add Up
2:15 The Louse That Exposed the Date
4:03 The Moroccan Cave With the First Tailor's Tools
5:52 The Needle That Unlocked the Cold World
7:24 The People Who Skipped Clothes in the Cold
9:09 The Tropical Bubble You Live In
10:24 The Hitchhiker That Came With Your Shirt

RESEARCH & SOURCES

▸ Kittler, Kayser & Stoneking (2003), Current Biology. Body lice split from head lice about 72,000 years ago, give or take 42,000. https://utsouthwestern.elsevierpure.com/en/publications/molecular-evolution-of-pediculus-humanus-and-the-origin-of-clothi

▸ Toups, Kitchen, Light & Reed (2011), Molecular Biology and Evolution. Clothing lice diverged at least 83,000 and possibly 170,000 years ago. https://doi.org/10.1093/molbev/msq234

▸ Hallett et al. (2021), iScience. Bone tools and skinned carnivores at Contrebandiers Cave, Morocco, 120,000–90,000 years ago. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8478944

▸ Soressi et al. (2013), PNAS. Neanderthal bone hide-smoothers in France. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3761603

▸ Gilligan, d’Errico, Doyon, Wang & Kuzmin (2024). Earliest eyed needles and early clothing. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11212769

▸ Collard et al. (2016), Journal of Anthropological Archaeology. Cape-like versus specialized cold-weather clothing. https://abdn.elsevierpure.com/en/publications/faunal-evidence-for-a-difference-in-clothing-use-between-neandert/

▸ Gilligan (2007), World Archaeology. Neanderthal extinction and clothing. https://researchportalplus.anu.edu.au/en/publications/neanderthal-extinction-and-modern-human-behaviour-the-role-of-cli/

▸ Denisova Cave needle report (2016). https://archaeology.org/news/2016/08/23/160823-denisova-cave-needle/

▸ Watanabe et al. (2021), Scientific Reports. Bone density, genes and brown fat in the Fuegians. https://orca.cardiff.ac.uk/147761/1/s41598-021-02783-1.pdf

▸ Cold acclimation recruits human brown fat (2013), Journal of Clinical Investigation. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3726172

▸ Brown fat and cold-induced thermogenesis (skeptical view). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6250802


────────────────────

PEOPLE, SITES & TERMS MENTIONED IN THIS VIDEO

▸ Mark Stoneking: geneticist whose team used lice DNA to date the origin of clothing
▸ David Reed: University of Florida researcher who re-dated the lice split with more genes
▸ Emily Hallett: researcher who led the study of the Contrebandiers Cave bone tools
▸ Marie Soressi: archaeologist who described Neanderthal bone smoothers in France
▸ Matt Pope: University College London archaeologist who explains why smoothed leather makes better clothing
▸ Ian Gilligan: researcher who surveyed eyed needles and proposed the clothing and Neanderthal idea
▸ Mikiko Watanabe: lead author of the Tierra del Fuego bone density and DNA study
▸ Wouter van Marken Lichtenbelt: Maastricht University researcher who studied brown fat and mild cold
▸ Contrebandiers Cave: Atlantic coast of Morocco, near Temara
▸ Denisova Cave: Siberia, site of an eyed bone needle found with Denisovan remains
▸ Yaghan (Tierra del Fuego): hunter-gatherers described as wearing no closed clothing in a cold climate
▸ Molecular clock: counts DNA changes that build up at a roughly steady rate, so more differences mean more time apart
▸ Brown fat: a tissue that burns energy to make heat

────────────────────

NOTE: Several ideas here are hypotheses, not settled facts: the lice-based date of the first clothes (the error bars are huge), the cave tools as evidence of clothing (suggestive, not proof), Gilligan's idea that clothing helped Neanderthals vanish, and brown fat as the Fuegians' secret. Each is debated, and plenty of researchers think Neanderthals dressed far better than that idea gives them credit for. Some work suggests brown fat adds little to how many calories adults burn. Nobody knows what the very first piece of clothing was for, because fur, leather and fiber rot. This video is educational and is not medical advice.

If this changed how you see what you're wearing, like the video, comment which fact surprised you most, and subscribe for more ancient human mysteries.
